meaning: To do or say something that eases a stiff start and lets people talk.
example: She opened with a short story from the train ride, just enough to break the ice before the hard question.
origin: By the 1590s it already meant making a start. Shakespeare uses it that way in The Taming of the Shrew.

meaning: Something easy to do.
example: After three rehearsals, the opening minute was a piece of cake. The close was not.

meaning: Arriving or acting late is still better than not doing it at all.
example: The apology came after the vote, and still it mattered: better late than never.
origin: A proverb in English since the Middle Ages.

meaning: To stop working on something for now.
example: We had the outline and the examples. He called it a day rather than sanding the same sentence again.

meaning: Sharing the same understanding of a plan or a fact.
example: Before we argue the motion, I want us on the same page about what the budget actually says.

meaning: To say the important part without a long windup.
example: The chair tapped the table and asked her to get to the point before the room drifted.

meaning: Only later events will show whether this was right.
example: We can guess at the treaty's cost tonight. Time will tell whether the towns can live with it.

meaning: To decide, and stop hovering between choices.
example: The district is watching. Make up your mind before the other side writes the choice for you.

meaning: Listening closely and ready to hear more.
example: Tell us what you saw in the ward. We are all ears.

meaning: To watch something carefully so it does not go wrong.
example: Keep an eye on the amendment. A quiet clause can undo the whole bill.

idiom: hit the nail on the head
meaning: To describe a problem or a truth with exact accuracy.
example: When she said the town was not short of plans but of follow-through, she hit the nail on the head.
origin: An old carpentry image for a blow that lands exactly where it should.

idiom: the ball is in your court
meaning: It is your turn to act or to answer.
example: We sent the revised offer this morning. The ball is in your court.
origin: From tennis: the ball is on the other player's side, so the next shot is theirs.

meaning: To start an activity so that others can join and keep it going.
example: A single signed letter will get the ball rolling. The rest of the block can add their names tonight.
origin: It comes from games in which players keep a ball moving, and later from campaigns that opened a drive the same way.

meaning: In a few words; the short version of something larger.
example: In a nutshell, the levy fixes the bridge and nothing else.
origin: Pliny describes a copy of the Iliad small enough to fit inside a nutshell. The phrase came to mean 'in brief.'

meaning: Feeling ill, or not at full strength.
example: He looked under the weather and still took the evening meeting, which did the argument no favors.

meaning: Very rarely.
example: This council admits a mistake once in a blue moon. Tonight should be that night.

meaning: The latest small trouble that makes a stacked burden too much to bear.
example: The delayed bus was only the last straw. The route had been failing for a year.
origin: From the proverb about the last straw that breaks the camel's back.

meaning: Never; used to say a promise is not believable.
example: They will publish the full costs when pigs fly, unless we ask for them in public.

meaning: What people do is better evidence than what they say.
example: Actions speak louder than words. The vacant inspector post tells us more than the press release.
origin: An old proverb: what a person does outweighs what they claim.

meaning: A little extra caution now is wiser than regret later.
example: Bring the paper copy. Better safe than sorry if the hall's network drops.

meaning: To skip the buildup and go straight to what matters.
example: I will cut to the chase: we cannot staff the clinic on last year's number.
origin: From early film editing, when a story skipped the dialogue and cut to the chase scene.

meaning: To learn how a job or a place actually works.
example: Give her a month to learn the ropes before you judge the brief.
origin: On a sailing ship, a new sailor had to learn which rope did what.

meaning: To be too late for an opportunity.
example: If we wait for a perfect draft, we will miss the boat on this session.

meaning: In a risky position where one more mistake could bring failure.
example: The department is on thin ice with the families it already failed once.

meaning: To refuse to take a side.
example: You can sit on the fence through the hearing. You cannot sit there through the vote.

meaning: The whole situation, not only one detail.
example: A cheaper bulb is not the big picture. The big picture is a street people will walk after dark.

meaning: Not yet decided.
example: The site is still up in the air, so do not promise a groundbreaking date.

meaning: To make a conflict or a problem worse.
example: A sarcastic reply will only add fuel to the fire. Answer the charge.

idiom: at the end of the day
meaning: When everything else is considered; the point that remains.
example: We can trade adjectives all night. At the end of the day, the shelter has twelve beds and forty names.

meaning: To avoid saying something directly.
example: Do not beat around the bush about the shortfall. Name the number.
origin: Hunters beat the bushes to drive birds into the open instead of going straight at them.

idiom: bite off more than you can chew
meaning: To take on more work or responsibility than you can finish.
example: Three new programs in one quarter is biting off more than this office can chew.
origin: American English, from taking a larger plug of chewing tobacco than your mouth can manage.

meaning: To become uncontrolled.
example: Stop the rumor before it gets out of hand. A correction tomorrow is already late.

meaning: To try something, without a guarantee of success.
example: The old route failed. Give the evening bus a shot for one semester and then count the riders.

meaning: In trouble for something you did.
example: He knew the missing disclosure would land the firm in hot water, and he said so before the letter arrived.

meaning: It is not as complicated as people are making it.
example: Label the allergen on the menu. It's not rocket science, and it keeps a child out of the emergency room.
origin: Late twentieth-century American English, treating rocket science as the model of difficult technical work.

meaning: To free someone from blame or from a duty they still owe.
example: A vague apology lets the agency off the hook. Ask who signed the order.
origin: From fishing: a fish that slips free of the hook.

meaning: Progress costs real effort or discomfort.
example: No pain, no gain is a poor slogan for a budget cut. Some pain is only waste.
origin: The older English proverb is 'no pains, no gains.'

meaning: Strictly according to the rules.
example: File it by the book. A shortcut here becomes the other side's exhibit.

meaning: Using exactly the same words, with nothing changed.
example: Read the warning word for word. A paraphrase will soften the part people need to hear.

meaning: To recover your composure and act with control.
example: Pull yourself together before you take the microphone. The room needs a steady voice, not a shaken one.

meaning: Back to the start, with the progress lost.
example: If the grant falls through, the clinic is back to square one on the roof.

idiom: cost an arm and a leg
meaning: To cost far too much.
example: The marble lobby would cost an arm and a leg and would not treat a single patient.

meaning: Something gained quickly or casually is easily lost the same way.
example: Easy come, easy go is how the surplus vanished: a windfall in, a dozen pet projects out.

meaning: Repeating a skill is how you get good at it.
example: Practice makes perfect, which is why the opening should be said aloud and not only admired on the page.

meaning: Stay hopeful and don't let a setback crush you.
example: Keep your chin up. One lost vote is not the end of the ordinance.

meaning: To study seriously.
example: The interns can hit the books this weekend. Monday's hearing will not wait for a summary.

meaning: A way to wish someone well before a performance.
example: You know the closing story. Break a leg, and leave the extra joke out.

meaning: No matter what happens, or what the weather is.
example: The canvass goes ahead come rain or shine. People still eat on a wet Tuesday.

meaning: To agree.
example: We do not have to see eye to eye on the slogan to see eye to eye on the staffing number.
origin: The phrase is biblical, from Isaiah 52:8. In English it came to mean agreeing with someone.

meaning: To work late into the night.
example: The committee burned the midnight oil, and the dawn draft was still cleaner than the one they started with.
origin: From the oil lamps people worked by before electric light.

meaning: Caught in the act, with the evidence plain.
example: The inspector was caught red-handed altering the log. The denial did not survive the timestamp.
origin: From older Scottish law, where a person taken with blood still on the hand was caught in the act.

meaning: To destroy a way back so you cannot return to a former position or ally.
example: Resign in anger and you burn your bridges with the only office that can still fund the program.
origin: From armies that destroyed a bridge behind them, leaving no retreat.

meaning: The largest part of something, sometimes nearly all of it.
example: One contractor took the lion's share of the repairs and left the side streets waiting.
origin: In Aesop's fable the lion does not take the biggest piece. He takes every share.

meaning: Pretending you never wanted something after you fail to get it.
example: Calling the award meaningless is sour grapes. Last month he wanted it on the letterhead.
origin: From Aesop's fox, who calls the grapes sour when he cannot reach them.

meaning: To raise a false alarm so often that people stop believing a real one.
example: Do not cry wolf about every delay. Save the alarm for a deadline we will actually miss.
origin: From Aesop's shepherd, who shouts that a wolf is attacking until the village ignores the real wolf.

meaning: A very small amount compared with what is needed.
example: A single tutor is a drop in the bucket when the whole grade is behind in reading.
origin: From Isaiah 40:15, where the nations are called a drop in a bucket.

idiom: by the skin of your teeth
meaning: By the narrowest possible margin.
example: The appeal was filed by the skin of our teeth, with minutes left on the clock.
origin: The English phrase comes from the Book of Job: 'I am escaped with the skin of my teeth.'

meaning: To issue a direct challenge.
example: She threw down the gauntlet: debate the clause in public, or withdraw it.
origin: A medieval knight threw down his glove, the gauntlet, to challenge someone to fight.

meaning: To give someone a severe warning to stop misbehaving.
example: The principal read the riot act, and then she did the harder thing: she changed the dismissal plan.
origin: Britain's Riot Act of 1714 had to be read aloud to an unruly crowd before force could be used.

meaning: To take attention or credit that belonged to someone else.
example: Do not steal her thunder. She did the fieldwork; let her deliver the finding.
origin: In the early 1700s the playwright John Dennis heard a theater reuse his thunder effect and accused them of stealing his thunder.

idiom: the proof is in the pudding
meaning: You judge a thing by trying it, not by how it is advertised.
example: The proof is in the pudding. If ridership does not rise, the new schedule was a slogan.
origin: Shortened from the older proverb 'the proof of the pudding is in the eating,' recorded by the seventeenth century.

meaning: An unpredictable person whose actions can damage their own side.
example: A loose cannon on the podium can sink a careful case in a single ad-lib.
origin: A cannon that broke loose on a ship's deck could crush the crew as it rolled.

meaning: To prepare for trouble and secure what you can.
example: Batten down the hatches before the audit. Lock the files and write down who approved each change.
origin: Sailors battened down hatches, fastening the covers, before a storm.

meaning: Everyone available is needed to help.
example: The snow day is not a pause. It is all hands on deck to reach the families without heat.
origin: A ship's call for the whole crew to come up on deck.

meaning: Surprised and briefly thrown off balance.
example: The committee was taken aback by the vacancy rate, which no one had put in the briefing.
origin: A ship is taken aback when the wind suddenly hits the front of the sails and checks its way.

meaning: A clue or a topic that distracts from the real issue.
example: The typeface of the flyer is a red herring. The question is whether the claim in it is true.
origin: A cured herring has a strong smell that can draw hounds off a trail. The phrase came to mean a false lead.

meaning: To shift responsibility to someone else.
example: Do not pass the buck to a subcommittee that will not meet until after the deadline.
origin: In nineteenth-century American poker, a marker called a buck showed whose turn it was to deal, and a player could pass it on.

meaning: This is where responsibility is accepted, not handed onward.
example: The buck stops here. I approved the timeline, and I will explain the miss.
origin: Harry Truman kept this sentence on a desk sign so responsibility would not be passed along. It plays on the older poker phrase 'pass the buck.'

meaning: To quit because you cannot win or cannot continue.
example: Do not throw in the towel after one hostile headline. The votes are not cast.
origin: In boxing, a cornerman throws a towel into the ring to stop the fight.

meaning: To fight unfairly, often by attacking something personal.
example: Question the record. Hitting below the belt about his family will cost you the room.
origin: The Queensberry rules of boxing forbid a punch below the belt.

idiom: throw your hat in the ring
meaning: To announce that you are entering a contest.
example: She threw her hat in the ring only after the filing fee and the signatures were both real.
origin: A boxer threw a hat into the ring to accept a challenge. The image later moved into politics.

meaning: Close to defeat and struggling to recover.
example: The proposal is on the ropes. A clear amendment might save it; another speech will not.
origin: A boxer on the ropes is pinned at the edge of the ring and taking punches.

meaning: To adapt so that a setback does less damage.
example: Roll with the punches if the witness goes off script, and bring the panel back to the date on the invoice.
origin: A boxer rolls with a punch, moving with the blow so it lands with less force.

meaning: To prepare for every likely problem or duty.
example: Cover all the bases: the cost, the staffing, and what happens if the grant is late.
origin: From baseball, where fielders have to account for every base.

meaning: To take your turn and accept a hard responsibility.
example: Someone from this dais has to step up to the plate and move the funding, not just praise it.
origin: From baseball: the batter steps up to the plate when it is their turn to hit.

meaning: A rough estimate, good enough to plan with and not exact.
example: Give us a ballpark figure for the roof before we pretend the reserve can cover it.
origin: American English, from the kind of rough estimate a person might make while watching a baseball game.

meaning: To face something painful or difficult and get on with it.
example: We should bite the bullet and close the unsafe wing instead of painting over the cracks.

meaning: To pursue the wrong person or the wrong explanation.
example: If you blame the night clerk, you are barking up the wrong tree. The waiver was signed upstairs.
origin: From raccoon hunting, when a dog barks at a tree the animal has already left.

meaning: Something that looks unfortunate and later turns out to help.
example: Losing the rushed contract was a blessing in disguise. The second bid protected the town.
origin: The earliest known printed use is James Hervey's 1746 phrase 'blessings in disguise.'

meaning: A person who argues the opposing side so a case is tested, not because they hold that side.
example: Play devil's advocate for ten minutes. If the plan survives that, it is ready for the public.
origin: From the Catholic office, created in 1587, whose task was to argue against a candidate for sainthood.

meaning: Something that can help and harm at the same time.
example: A viral clip is a double-edged sword. It can carry the fact, and it can bury the fact under the joke.

meaning: An obvious problem that people are avoiding.
example: The elephant in the room is the unpaid overtime, not the color of the new badges.

idiom: give someone the benefit of the doubt
meaning: To treat a person as honest or correct when you are not yet sure.
example: Give the new clerk the benefit of the doubt once. Do not give it to a missing public record.
origin: From law: when the proof is uncertain, the decision goes to the accused.

meaning: Back to planning, because the attempt failed.
example: The pilot missed every target we set. It is back to the drawing board, not back to the press tour.
origin: Popularized by a 1941 New Yorker cartoon of a designer walking away from a crashed machine.

meaning: Sharing the same difficulty.
example: Renters and the small shops are in the same boat if the street stays closed through December.

meaning: To join a cause or a fashion because it is already popular.
example: Jump on the bandwagon after you have read the text, not because the hashtag is loud.
origin: From nineteenth-century American parades, when a band rode a wagon and supporters climbed aboard.

meaning: To leave a quiet trouble alone rather than stir it up.
example: Let sleeping dogs lie on the old boundary dispute, and spend the hour on the flood map.
origin: A medieval warning. Chaucer already says it is unwise to wake a sleeping hound.

meaning: Past the first danger, but not safe yet.
example: The injunction helps. We are not out of the woods until the full hearing.

meaning: Set aside for later while something more urgent is handled.
example: Put the logo on the back burner. The evacuation route is the work of this week.
origin: From cooking: a pot moved to a rear burner simmers while you tend what is in front.

meaning: The small visible part of a much larger problem.
example: These three complaints are the tip of the iceberg. The hotline log is the rest.
origin: Most of an iceberg sits underwater, so the part you see is the smaller danger.

meaning: To start behaving in a better way.
example: The agency can turn over a new leaf by publishing the queue, not by changing the slogan.
origin: A leaf is a page of a book. Turning over a new leaf meant starting on a fresh page.

idiom: two sides of the same coin
meaning: Two things that look different and are really parts of one fact.
example: Turnover and burnout are two sides of the same coin in this ward.

meaning: To survive a difficult period.
example: If we tell the truth early, the office can weather the storm. A late leak will be worse.
origin: From a ship that comes through a storm still afloat.

idiom: you can't have your cake and eat it too
meaning: You cannot keep something and also use it up.
example: You can't have your cake and eat it too: a tax cut and the same library hours will not both survive the year.
origin: An old proverb. The earlier wording, 'eat your cake and have it,' makes the contradiction plain.

idiom: between a rock and a hard place
meaning: Facing two bad choices, with no comfortable third.
example: Raise the fare and riders leave; freeze it and the route is cut. We are between a rock and a hard place.

meaning: To do something that has not been done before.
example: The evening clinic would break new ground in this county. Say that plainly, and say what it costs.
origin: From plowing land that has not been farmed before.

meaning: To save time or money by skipping a necessary step.
example: Cut corners on the paint, not on the fire doors.

meaning: Until the last possible moment.
example: The count went down to the wire, and the margin was forty-one votes.
origin: From horse racing, where a wire marked the finish line.

meaning: To do more than what is required.
example: Go the extra mile for the translation. Half the block will not hear the plan in English alone.
origin: From the Sermon on the Mount: if someone compels you to go one mile, go a second.

meaning: To start too soon.
example: Do not jump the gun with a victory speech. The absentee ballots are still sealed.
origin: From track racing, where a runner who starts before the gun has jumped it.

idiom: lay your cards on the table
meaning: To say openly what you want and what you know.
example: Lay your cards on the table about the conflict of interest before someone else does it for you.
origin: From card games, where showing your cards ends the hiding.

meaning: To compromise, with each side giving up part of what it wanted.
example: We can meet them halfway on the timeline. We should not meet them halfway on the safety test.

meaning: To decide as the situation develops, without a fixed plan.
example: Play the opening by the script and play the questions by ear.
origin: From playing music without written notes, adjusting as you hear it.

idiom: put the cart before the horse
meaning: To do a step before the one it depends on.
example: Naming the building before you fund the staff puts the cart before the horse.
origin: An old proverb, in English since the 1500s, for reversing the order of two steps.

meaning: To disturb a situation that others want left alone.
example: Someone has to rock the boat. A quiet room is how the overcharge lasted six years.

meaning: To refuse to retreat from a position you believe is right.
example: Stand your ground on the public record. Courtesy does not require you to hide the number.

meaning: The advantages of two different choices at once.
example: Remote testimony gives us the best of both worlds only if the witness can still be cross-examined.

meaning: A past conflict that is no longer worth fighting.
example: The 2019 slogan is water under the bridge. The unpaid invoices are not.

meaning: With obvious, complete success.
example: The clinic passed the inspection with flying colors, and the report should be posted today.
origin: A ship that came through a fight with its flags still flying had won. The phrase now means succeeding openly.

meaning: To focus tightly on a target or a cause.
example: Zero in on the discharge date. The rest of the chart is background.
origin: From gunnery: to zero a weapon is to set its sights on the target.

idiom: speak softly and carry a big stick
meaning: Negotiate calmly, and keep real power in reserve so the calm is credible.
example: Speak softly and carry a big stick: offer the extension, and be ready to enforce the fine if it is refused.
origin: Theodore Roosevelt's maxim for quiet dealing backed by the power to act.

meaning: To take an irreversible step.
example: Filing the complaint crosses the Rubicon. After that, there is no quiet retreat.
origin: In 49 BC Julius Caesar led his army across the Rubicon into Italy. After that crossing he could not turn back.

meaning: The one weakness in something otherwise strong.
example: The report's Achilles' heel is the sample size. Everything else in it holds.
origin: From the later Greek myth that Achilles could be wounded only on the heel.

meaning: To start a process that releases many troubles you cannot put back.
example: A blanket subpoena will open Pandora's box of private records the hearing does not need.
origin: In Greek myth Pandora opened a jar, later called a box, and released troubles into the world.

idiom: a leopard cannot change its spots
meaning: A person's settled character does not flip because of a speech.
example: A leopard cannot change its spots, but a board can change its chair. Judge the record, then judge the vote.
origin: From the Book of Jeremiah, which asks whether a leopard can change its spots.

meaning: A clear sign that failure or the end is coming.
example: The writing on the wall was the third empty shift. The closure announcement only confirmed it.
origin: From Daniel 5, where a hand writes a warning on the wall of Belshazzar's feast.

meaning: A hidden weakness under a grand reputation.
example: The hero of the industry had feet of clay: the safety log had been rewritten for years.
origin: From Daniel 2, the great statue whose feet are partly clay and cannot hold it up.

meaning: A person or thing you cherish above others.
example: The reading hour is the apple of her eye, which is why cutting it will not pass quietly.
origin: A biblical image for someone cherished. The apple is the pupil of the eye.

meaning: A dangerous person or plan disguised as something harmless.
example: A fee called a convenience charge can be a wolf in sheep's clothing.
origin: From the Sermon on the Mount, which warns of false prophets who come in sheep's clothing but are wolves.

meaning: To fail completely, or to be defeated.
example: Three of the amendments will bite the dust. Spend your speech on the one that can pass.
origin: An old image, familiar from translations of Homer, of a fallen fighter face down in the dust.

meaning: Very drunk.
example: He arrived three sheets to the wind, and the committee wisely did not let him speak.
origin: On a ship, a sheet is a rope that controls a sail. Loose sheets leave the boat unsteady, like a drunk person.

meaning: A carried grudge that makes you quick to take offense.
example: A chip on your shoulder will turn a fair question into a fight. Answer it.
origin: In nineteenth-century America, a boy would set a wood chip on his shoulder and dare someone to knock it off.

meaning: Rescued from failure by a timely interruption.
example: The motion was saved by the bell when the session adjourned before the bad amendment came up.
origin: From boxing: a fighter on the canvas is spared a loss when the round's bell rings.

meaning: To tackle a painful problem directly.
example: Grasp the nettle. Name the contaminated well before the company names a scapegoat.
origin: A nettle stings less when you take hold of it firmly, so the proverb means meeting a difficulty head-on.

meaning: To search or try every possibility.
example: Leave no stone unturned on the chain of custody. One unsigned bag can lose the case.
origin: An ancient Greek saying for a search that misses nothing.

idiom: separate the wheat from the chaff
meaning: To tell what is valuable from what is worthless.
example: Separate the wheat from the chaff in that inbox. Two letters are evidence. The rest are noise.
origin: From the old image of winnowing grain, used in the Bible, where wind carries off the chaff and the wheat remains.

idiom: take it with a grain of salt
meaning: To treat a claim with caution rather than full belief.
example: Take the anonymous poll with a grain of salt, and ask who paid for it.
origin: Pliny the Elder describes a poison antidote to be taken with a grain of salt. The phrase came to mean hearing a claim skeptically.

meaning: When a situation is serious and the decision finally counts.
example: When the chips are down, a prepared witness is worth more than a clever slogan.
origin: From poker: the chips are the stakes, and when they are down the hand is being played for real.

meaning: To make a bad situation worse by adding an offense on top of the harm.
example: The fine was the injury. Publishing the worker's home address added insult to injury.
origin: The idea is in a fable by Phaedrus: a man hurts himself trying to swat a fly, and the fly treats that as a further slight.

meaning: In a state of confusion or disorder.
example: The office was at sixes and sevens on the morning of the vote, which is how the wrong draft went out.

meaning: On the whole; generally, allowing for exceptions.
example: By and large the pilots worked. The two that failed need a public explanation, not a shrug.
origin: Sailors said 'by' for sailing into the wind and 'large' for sailing with it. By and large meant in all conditions, and then 'generally.'

idiom: burn the candle at both ends
meaning: To exhaust yourself by working or living too hard, especially by losing sleep.
example: She is burning the candle at both ends. A tired advocate drops the citation the case depends on.
origin: An old proverb for using up a candle, and your strength, from both ends at once.

meaning: Spoken without preparation.
example: An off-the-cuff number will be quoted as policy. If you do not know it, say so.
origin: From speakers who jotted quick notes on a shirt cuff and then talked from them.

meaning: To use every resource you have.
example: Pull out all the stops for the evacuation drill, including the radio station and the church vans.
origin: On a pipe organ, pulling out the stops lets more pipes sound, up to the full instrument.

meaning: To find a meaning that is implied and not stated.
example: Read between the lines of the resignation. 'More time with family' arrived the week the audit opened.

idiom: take the bull by the horns
meaning: To confront a difficulty directly and with courage.
example: Take the bull by the horns and open with the deficit. The room already knows it is there.
origin: A proverb for meeting a danger the way a handler controls a bull, by the horns.

meaning: Through good times and bad; with loyalty that does not quit.
example: She stayed with the clinic through thick and thin, including the year the grant was frozen.
origin: The older English picture is travel through thicket and thin wood, the hard ground and the easier.

meaning: To reverse a situation so the other side is now at a disadvantage.
example: The new receipt turned the tables. The accuser had to explain his own signature.
origin: From games such as backgammon, once called tables, when the board turned and the positions reversed.

meaning: Good enough to meet the required standard.
example: The first draft is not up to scratch. The dates disagree with the exhibits.
origin: In early prizefighting, a fighter had to come up to a line scratched on the ground in order to continue.

meaning: To win easily.
example: On the safety vote she will win hands down. The budget vote is the fight.
origin: In horse racing, a jockey who is winning easily can drop the hands and loosen the reins.

meaning: Wait. Do not rush ahead.
example: Hold your horses on the press release until counsel has read the second paragraph.
origin: A literal warning to a driver, which became a call for patience.

idiom: make hay while the sun shines
meaning: To act while conditions are favorable.
example: The chair is sympathetic this month. Make hay while the sun shines and file the bill.
origin: A farming proverb: cut and dry the hay while the weather allows.

meaning: To stop being careful and take a risk.
example: Do not throw caution to the wind with an unnamed source. One document is a better gamble.

idiom: keep your cards close to the vest
meaning: To keep your plans or information secret.
example: Keep your cards close to the vest until the witness is sworn. A preview only helps the other table.
origin: From poker and other card games, where you hold the cards against your vest so no one can see them.

idiom: pull the wool over someone's eyes
meaning: To deceive someone.
example: A glossy chart can pull the wool over a tired committee's eyes. Ask for the raw count.

meaning: Said when someone you have just been talking about appears.
example: Speak of the devil. We were just asking who approved the overtime, and here is the signature.
origin: From the old warning that speaking of the devil might make him appear. It is now said when a person you just mentioned walks in.

meaning: A hard barrier that cuts one people or region off from another.
example: Secrecy dropped an iron curtain between the agency and the families it serves.
origin: Churchill's 1946 speech at Fulton, Missouri, made this the name for Europe's Cold War divide. The image was already in circulation; that speech fixed it.

idiom: a house divided against itself cannot stand
meaning: A group split by a fundamental conflict cannot last.
example: A house divided against itself cannot stand. A board that will not share one set of numbers cannot run one hospital.
origin: The sentence is from the Gospels. Abraham Lincoln used it in 1858 to say the United States could not remain half slave and half free.

meaning: A sharp choice between political participation and violence.
example: He framed the registration drive as the ballot or the bullet, and then he spent the hour on how to register.
origin: Malcolm X's 1964 speech of this name set the vote against violence as the choice in front of Black Americans.

meaning: A powerful public office used to persuade people, not only to govern them.
example: The mayor still has a bully pulpit. Use it on the bus cuts before the hearing, not after the route is gone.
origin: Theodore Roosevelt's name for the presidency as a superb platform for argument. In his mouth, bully meant excellent.
